title: Bank of Japan is expected to hold rates this week — but stay hawkish: CNBC survey
description: Kazuo Ueda, governor of the Bank of Japan (BOJ), speaks during a conference hosted by the bank's Institute for Monetary and Economic Studies in Tokyo,
body: Kazuo Ueda, governor of the Bank of Japan (BOJ), speaks during a conference hosted by the bank's Institute for Monetary and Economic Studies in Tokyo, Japan, on Tuesday, May 27, 2025. Kiyoshi Ota | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Bank of Japan is expected to keep the policy rate unchanged at 1.25% at the end of its two-day meeting on Friday, according to a CNBC survey, with the possibility of a hike very much alive in the coming months.All 16 respondents expect the BOJ to stand pat, given the bank raised rates last month to their highest level in 31 years. All respondents said they expect the BOJ to set the stage for a rate hike in December or January next year, as domestic inflation and wages continue to rise. Macroeconomic factors support the BOJ's additional policy tightening, said Homin Lee, senior macro strategist at Lombard Odier. "But there may not be sufficient consensus in the policy board for successive rate hikes given the fragility in the domestic bond market," he added. Sosuke Nakamura, an economist at Citi Research, said he sees no clear signs of inflation accelerating to a degree that would justify consecutive rate hikes. Japan's core inflation, excluding fresh foods, for September rose 2.1% from a year earlier, reaching its highest this year as a weak yen raises import costs and elevated energy costs feed through to higher prices, even as government subsidies absorb rising costs of energy for consumers. Japan's inflation-adjusted wages rose for the eighth month in a row in August, climbing 1.5% from a year earlier, according to the most recent government data, signaling potential wage-growth-driven inflation as well.Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama reportedly told lawmakers last week that Japan was "on the cusp of shifting to a period of sustained inflation driven by rising wages," while acknowledging that higher import costs were also pushing up prices.The BOJ is expected to declare that its "underlying inflation" target of 2% has been met at this meeting, according to reports by Reuters and The Japan Times. Yen and yields Ryutaro Kimura, senior fixed income strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management, said he was waiting to see if the BOJ changes its phrasing about inflation in the monetary policy statement this week from "underlying CPI inflation has been approaching 2 percent" to it "has reached 2 percent."As for the yen, nine respondents expect it to trade between 157 and 158 against the greenback over the next one month. Respondents' outlook for the three-month yen target was more scattered, ranging from 150 to 160."BOJ normalization, higher domestic yields and shifting institutional flows should gradually narrow the rate differential and pull capital back toward Japan," said Masahiko Loo, senior fixed income strategist at State Street Investment Management. But he added, "Elevated U.S. yields should prevent a straight-line yen rally."The yen strengthened against the dollar, and Japanese government bond yields fell last week due to safe-haven demand amid a sell-off in AI stocks —  a reversal from earlier in the month, when Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's spending plans and a global bond sell-off pressured those assets. Nine respondents said they expect the yield on the benchmark 10-year JGBs to be between 3% and 3.1% by the end of the year, up from the current 2.809%. Seven respondents said they expect the yield on the 30-year JGB to rise to 4% to 4.1% from 3.829% as of Tuesday. That forecast comes as analysts expect the BOJ will resume tightening after an anticipated pause in October. Takuji Aida, chief Japan economist at Credit Agricole, said the next rate hike is likely to happen in January, when the BOJ is scheduled to release its quarterly outlook report that assesses economic activity and prices. Thirteen respondents said they expect a terminal rate, or the level at which the BOJ is expected to stop its tightening cycle, of 1.75% to 2% by around mid-2027. Macroeconomic data shows the policy rate is closer to the neutral level of 2%, the BOJ's inflation target, said Masato Koike, senior economist at SOMPO Institute Plus. But "given the state of the Japanese economy and the need to avoid excessive downward pressure on growth, I expect the BOJ to stop raising rates at around 1.75%," Koike said. The CNBC survey was conducted from Oct. 14  to 26 among 16 economists and analysts.— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie and Sri Jegarajah contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Bank of Japan is expected to hold rates this week — but stay hawkish: CNBC survey

title: Israeli election draws tens of thousands of citizens flying back to vote
description: An El Al Boeing 737-958(ER) takes off from Barcelona-El Prat Airport in Barcelona, Spain, on Aug. 27, 2025. Joan Valls | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesAn ext
body: An El Al Boeing 737-958(ER) takes off from Barcelona-El Prat Airport in Barcelona, Spain, on Aug. 27, 2025. Joan Valls | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesAn extremely tight race into Israel's election Tuesday, has some citizens flying back into the country to cast their votes.Israel doesn't allow votes from abroad, except from those serving in the country's diplomatic missions. As many as 80,000 Israelis living outside the country are expected to come back to vote in Tuesday's election, according to estimates from one group helping to organize citizens living outside the country. Israel has about 7.3 million eligible voters, according to the Washington-based International Foundation for Electoral Systems."While not a large block, the 80,000 that may return home to participate could make a big difference in the final count of a very tight election," said Yael Shomer, a professor of political science at Tel Aviv University.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks during a press conference, amid the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran, in Jerusalem, March 19, 2026. Ronen Zvulun | ReutersIn Israel's first election since 2022, Benjamin Netanyahu of the Likud party, who has served as Prime Minister for 18 years over three separate periods, is facing top challenger Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, who heads the Yashar party. Both would likely need backing from potential coalition partners in order to win. Polls are extremely tight heading into Tuesday's election. Issues like security, already a major decider for Israelis, have gotten even more contentious with the Iran war in full swing. The exemption of some ultra-Orthodox men from conscription is also causing a great divide in Israeli society, while Prime Minister Netanyahu is still working on a controversial plan that would give the governing coalition more control over the judiciary.25 October 2026, Israel, Tel Aviv: Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot addresses attendees from behind a lectern emblazoned with party slogans during an election rally. Erik Marmor | Picture Alliance | Getty Images"All elections in Israel are energetic, but because this one will have such a meaningful impact on the future of the country it has been especially hard fought," Shomer said. "This election is really about how we see our future, voter turnout will be very high."Voter turnout in 2022 was just above 70% according to Israel's Central Elections Committee. Pollsters believe it could reach as high as 87% this time. Among foreign service workers serving in embassies and consulates outside of Israel, voter turnout was 90%. According to The Central Elections Committee, that number is usually closer to 70%.In order to help those living abroad come back to cast votes, an organization called Fly & Vote was set up by the America-Israel Democracy Coalition, a U.S.-based group which was originally created in 2023 to stop the effort by Likud to reform the judicial system. While organizations and political parties are prohibited from paying for any kind of transportation for people inside or outside of Israel, Aid Coalition has found other ways to facilitate the voting. Fly & Vote, which has been funded by private donations, chartered a flight for Israelis living in Portugal and bought blocks of tickets for flights from the New York area. Anyone on the flights had to pay for their own seats. "Israelis who don't live here still have a stake in what we do, and we want to help them," said Ora Peled-Nakash, the group's co-founder. "We don't take a political position though and we don't tell anyone how to vote, we just help them cast their ballot." Travelers will also have plenty of commercial options.For decades El Al was the only Israeli airline to fly routes from the U.S. to Israel. Arkia started offering flights last year and Israir earlier this year. Legacy U.S. carriers United and Delta are also flying to Israel again after suspending flights due to the war with Iran. Germany's Lufthansa flies to Israel from Europe and British Airways is scheduled to re-start flights this week. What's more, the price is in line with what it would be during normal times, Peled-Nakash said. There were still a few seats left on El Al flights from JFK or Newark airports ranging from $1,300 to $2,500 as of Sunday, according to research from CNBC.After years of political instability that saw five elections between 2019 and 2022, Tueday's election result could help shape Israel's political, security and economic direction for years to come. But it also shows how politically divided the country has become.

schema.headline: Israeli election draws tens of thousands of citizens flying back to vote

title: JetBlue posts bigger loss on fuel costs, but CEO says margins improving
description: JetBlue planes populate the tarmac on June 24, 2026 at JFK Airport in the Queens borough of New York City.  Bruce Bennett | Getty ImagesJetBlue Airway
body: JetBlue planes populate the tarmac on June 24, 2026 at JFK Airport in the Queens borough of New York City.  Bruce Bennett | Getty ImagesJetBlue Airways reported a bigger loss in the third quarter compared with last year, but the New York carrier said strong travel demand is helping to offset higher fuel prices as it seeks to calm investors after shares fell to a new low Monday.JetBlue stock soared roughly 11% in after-hours trading Monday.JetBlue on Monday posted a net loss of $257 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a loss of $143 million a year earlier. The carrier's fuel bill rose 61% to $868 million. "Resilient demand and strong yields drove revenue well ahead of our initial expectations, allowing us to recapture more of the increase in fuel costs than we initially expected," CEO Joanna Geraghty said in an earnings release. "That momentum has carried into the fourth quarter, and Fort Lauderdale continues to deliver exceptional results even as we significantly grow capacity."JetBlue's average fares rose more than 19% to $245.11 in the third quarter from $205.67 in the year-earlier period.JetBlue executives are set to hold an earnings call on Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET, where they will face questions from analysts about the company's long-term health amid sustained losses. A group of the airline's senior creditors is reportedly working with restructuring adviser PJT Partners, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday.The carrier said it ended the quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing Monday."Importantly, we believe we have the liquidity and financing options to create a strong bridge to at least $1 EPS and positive free cash flow in 2028," CFO Ursula Hurley said in a statement. "We remain focused on disciplined cost execution and capital management as we work toward sustained profitability and positive free cash flow."Here is what JetBlue reported in the third quarter compared with Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG:Loss per share: 60 cents adjusted vs. a loss of 55 cents expectedRevenue: $2.81 billion vs. $2.82 billion expectedJetBlue last posted an annual profit in 2019. The airline is in the middle of a multiyear turnaround plan that includes cutting cuts and boosting revenue by investing in premium seats, like a new domestic first class section that recently went on sale.Fuel costs have eaten into airline profits across the board. JetBlue said travel demand has remained strong despite higher fares, which are up more than 20% this year.JetBlue has struggled not just with higher costs but also with competition from larger rivals. It sought to acquire now-defunct carrier Spirit Airlines, but that deal was upended by a federal judge who ruled it was anticompetitive. A judge also blocked a regional partnership between JetBlue and American Airlines, which the airlines argued would help them compete better against carriers in the congested Northeast U.S. JetBlue now has a partnership with United Airlines.

schema.headline: JetBlue posts bigger loss on fuel costs, but CEO says margins improving

title: Meta announces $95 billion stock offering to fund AI expansion
description: Meta said Monday it is planning to raise a total of $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure and superintellig
body: Meta said Monday it is planning to raise a total of $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure and superintelligence.The stock was down 1.6% in morning trading after the announcement. Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom were interested in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares, Meta said in a statement.The tech giant will initially raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, before raising an additional $60 billion with an at-the-market program.The news comes as hyperscalers pour record sums into the AI infrastructure build-out. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related capital spending could total about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031, across compute, data centers and power.Meta's planned investments will support "emerging AI opportunities" including its family of apps, its AI agent Muse and its data center business, the company said Monday.It plans to balance funding for these investments through a mix of operating cash flow, investment-grade debt, partnerships and equity capital.Meta racing to secure AI infrastructureMeta is among the major hyperscalers that are increasingly tapping debt to fund the expensive infrastructure required for the AI boom.Last week, Meta posted third-quarter results showing revenue jumped 26% year on year: $64.60 billion versus the $63.37 billion analysts expected. However, investors focused more on the tech company's negative free cash flow and its higher full-year capital expenditure forecast.It now expects its full-year capex to range from $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from $130 billion. That sent Meta's shares lower on Thursday. Meta is building four "superclusters" with more than 1 gigawatt of capacity each and is on track to nearly double total infrastructure capacity in 2026 on a year-over-year basis, the company said.The decision to raise more money "reflects the eye-watering levels of investment required to keep up in the AI arms race," Ben Wood, senior partner at CCS Insight, told CNBC. "Meta offering more stock comes at a time when numerous companies, such as Google, SpaceX and soon, Anthropic, are going to the markets to raise funds."Alphabet, Google's parent company, said it would look to raise $85 billion in June. SpaceX has closed a $40 billion debt financing to purchase graphics processing units. Anthropic is preparing for an initial public offering.TikTok U.S. is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity over the coming years, CNBC reported Friday.

schema.headline: Meta announces $95 billion stock offering to fund AI expansion

title: Lula wins Brazil runoff after prediction markets favored Bolsonaro
description: Brazil's President and presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva waves a national flag during a campaign rally in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on Sept. 2
body: Brazil's President and presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva waves a national flag during a campaign rally in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on Sept. 26, 2026. Miguel Schincariol | Afp | Getty ImagesLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva was reelected president of Brazil on Sunday in a runoff election, an upset that prediction markets odds failed to anticipate.Lula defeated Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-wing candidate and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, by 51.8% to 48.2%, according to the country's Superior Electoral Court. As late as Sunday afternoon, Lula remained a significant underdog on prediction markets. Even just after 8:30 p.m. ET on Sunday, Lula's odds were at 21% on Kalshi. Bolsonaro's odds on prediction markets surged after first-round voting on Oct. 4, with both Kalshi and Polymarket giving Bolsonaro an over 80% chance of ousting Lula. The Kalshi contract asked, "Brazil Presidential election winner?" and was verified by reporting from the Associated Press. Kalshi co-founder and CEO Tarek Mansour has previously defended Kalshi's election contracts. In August, Kalshi reflected a 95% likelihood of Wisconsin Democratic socialist Francesca Hong winning the Democratic gubernatorial primary over Milwaukee County executive David Crowley. Instead, Hong lost the race by less than 1 percentage point. "Before the 'prediction markets got it wrong' headlines roll in: a 5% probability doesn't mean it won't happen," Mansour wrote in an Aug. 12 social media post on X. "It means it should happen 1 in 20 times. If 5% candidates never won, the markets would be broken."Odds and prediction market platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls.Unlike prediction market odds, which pointed to a clear Bolsonaro victory, political polls showed a tight race in the days leading up to the contest.Brazil's Supreme Court also extended voting for two hours late Sunday, which Bolsonaro argued hurt his chances of winning the presidency. Bolsonaro is expected to challenge the outcome, Reuters reported. Following Lula's victory, Brazil-linked stocks and ETFs slid on Monday. The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) shed 22%, while U.S.-traded shares of Itau Unibanco and Banco Bradesco tanked 20% and nearly 30%, respectively. Brewer Ambev and Petrobras each declined more than 15%. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Lula wins Brazil runoff after prediction markets favored Bolsonaro

title: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
description: The icebreaker Tor (right) at the port of Sabetta in the Kara Sea shoreline on the Yamal Peninsula in the Arctic circle, some 2450 km of Moscow.Kirill
body: The icebreaker Tor (right) at the port of Sabetta in the Kara Sea shoreline on the Yamal Peninsula in the Arctic circle, some 2450 km of Moscow.Kirill Kudryavtesev | AFP | Getty ImagesChina and Russia are tightening their grip on Arctic shipping routes, turning the rapidly warming region into a new geopolitical battleground with Europe.Moscow and Beijing last week have agreed to expand freight traffic along Arctic shipping corridors, increase services between their ports and deepen cooperation on building polar vessels. The agreement came after the EU unveiled a new Arctic strategy aimed at countering growing Russian and Chinese influence in the region.Although the competing moves underscore how the once-remote region is turning into a strategic prize, analysts said that Europe's ability to challenge the emerging China-Russia partnership remains limited, given Moscow's control over the main shipping corridor and Beijing's growing commercial clout.Europe cannot realistically challenge Chinese and Russian dominance of Arctic shipping in any meaningful timeframe.Alicia Garcia-HerreroAPAC & MEA Chief Economist, Natixis CIBThat's because Moscow controls the Northern Sea Route, including shipping permits, transit fees and a vast fleet of nuclear icebreakers, while Beijing provides the cargo, vessels and industrial capacity needed to develop the corridor, she added.Europe, by contrast, has limited icebreaker capacity and Arctic infrastructure, leaving it with little leverage to challenge the partnership despite its position as a major destination market.A new geopolitical fault line?The Northern Sea Route offers itself as an increasingly attractive alternative, as Middle East disruptions expose vulnerabilities in established shipping corridors.Cargo traveling between Asia and Europe through the Northern Sea Route could have its journey shortened to between 18 to 22 days, down approximately 35% from the 28 to 35 day journey through Suez, according to data provided by Fertmax FZCO.For Moscow, the route offers an opportunity to redirect energy exports toward Asia as Western sanctions constrain its access to European markets, said industry watchers whom CNBC spoke to. On the other hand, it provides Beijing another trade artery that could reduce reliance on traditional maritime chokepoints.David Roche, a veteran strategist at Quantum Strategy & Geonomics, said the Arctic's importance lies less in its potential to transform global shipping than in the deepening economic dependence between Russia and China."The significance of the arctic route is for Russian energy shipments to China, which will increase China's control over Russia in terms of Russia's dependence on China to sell its energy to compensate for losses of its gas markets in Europe," Roche highlighted.The EU has acknowledged the growing challenge, highlighting the region's strategic value in its strategy, as mentioned by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas last week.With Russia and China increasing their footprint and ambition, the Arctic has become a front line of global power competition.Kaja KallasForeign Policy Chief, European UnionCan Europe fight back?Europe isn't entirely without leverage. The EU's new strategy calls for expanding European icebreaker capacity, strengthening maritime surveillance and developing infrastructure linking Arctic trade networks to European markets.It also proposes a maritime security hub and greater protection for undersea cables, reflecting growing concerns about Russian military activity and threats to critical infrastructure.Yet those strengths may not be enough to overturn the structural advantages enjoyed by Moscow and Beijing, said experts.Garcia-Herrero said Europe's leverage largely rests on its position as a major destination market and the presence of large shipping companies that have avoided the Arctic because of environmental and commercial risks.Without a sustained industrial push that the EU has only begun to discuss, Europe can raise the commercial and regulatory costs of the route, but cannot prevent or replace the China-Russia partnership that now operates it.Alicia Garcia-HerreroAPAC & MEA Chief Economist, Natixis CIBEurope also faces a strategic dilemma: engaging with the emerging corridor could deepen its reliance on Russian-controlled infrastructure, even as it seeks to reduce Moscow's economic influence.Fertmax FZCO's former global head of research, Daeijin Lee said Western operators face sanctions, insurance and compliance complications that make the route considerably less attractive than it is for Chinese companies."The Arctic gives diversification, not independence," he said.A threat to global trade?For all the geopolitical attention, the Arctic remains a marginal player in global shipping.Roche estimates Arctic trade accounts for roughly 0.3% of global shipping today and could reach about 1% by 2030.Data from Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom and CNBC calculations based on UN Trade and Development figures similarly supports the 0.3% figure, with 37.02 million tonnes of cargo transiting the Northern Sea Route in 2025 compared to the 12.72 billion tonnes of global seaborne trade in 2024.Only 3.2 million tonnes of that cargo, or less than a tenth, involved vessels transiting the entire route, rather than shipments originating or terminating in the Russian Arctic, according to the Centre for High North Logistics.But traffic may be picking up, the latest September 2026 CHNL data showed. The route recorded 104 confirmed transit voyages carrying an estimated 3.7 million tonnes of cargo by the end of September, exceeding the 3.2 million tonnes recorded during the entire 2025 navigation season.Much of the existing traffic consists of Russian oil, liquefied natural gas and other commodities rather than international container shipments.However, the route also faces significant commercial hurdles. Ice conditions restrict navigation for much of the year, while specialized vessels, insurance premiums and Russian transit fees can erode savings from shorter voyages.Matthew Wright, an analyst at Kpler, said the route remains poorly suited to replacing established shipping corridors because operators need reliable, year-round services.Lee similarly expects the Arctic to develop primarily as a seasonal express route for selected high-value cargo rather than a replacement for Suez.However, climate change could shift the balance in the long-term.A study published in the WMU Journal of Maritime Affairs projected that melting Polar ice could increase the Northern Sea Route's annual transit capacity to between 127 million and 463 million tonnes by 2050.

schema.headline: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?

title: FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, alleging retailer overcharged shoppers
description: A Dollar General store in New York, US, on Tuesday, June 3, 2025. Adam Gray | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Federal Trade Commission said Monday that it
body: A Dollar General store in New York, US, on Tuesday, June 3, 2025. Adam Gray | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Federal Trade Commission said Monday that it filed a lawsuit along with 20 states accusing Dollar General of charging customers more than the prices it displays on shelves, price tags and in advertisements. Shares of Dollar General dropped about 4% after the FTC announced the lawsuit.The complaint alleges that thousands of Dollar General stores have "taken advantage of vulnerable shoppers by extracting millions of dollars in unlawful overcharges with insufficient safeguards to prevent the practice." It also argues that Dollar General has received "tens of thousands" of complaints from consumers about charging higher than advertised prices, but that it has not implemented policies to address the problem. The states joining the FTC in the lawsuit are Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin."Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last," said Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection. Dollar General did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The suit comes as shoppers look for discounts while they face elevated food and gas prices. Officials across the political spectrum also aim to show their efforts to protect consumers from high costs ahead of the midterm election next week.

schema.headline: FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, alleging retailer overcharged shoppers

title: Trump DOJ unlawfully fired Epstein prosecutor Maurene Comey, judge rules
description: A federal judge ruled Monday that the Department of Justice's firing last year of New York federal prosecutor Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FB
body: A federal judge ruled Monday that the Department of Justice's firing last year of New York federal prosecutor Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, was unlawful.Judge Jesse Furman, in his ruling, also granted Maurene Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay as an assistant U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York from her termination on July 16, 2025, through Dec. 20, 2025, when the judge inferred she accepted another job.The DOJ said it would appeal Furman's ruling in which the judge rejected the department's arguments that the attorney general had authority to dismiss Comey without cause. The case is in in U.S. District Court in Manhattan.Comey's lawyers, in a statement, said, "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law.""As the Court correctly held, to accept the government's argument about unlimited executive power 'would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system,'" the lawyers said. "This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law."Before her termination, Comey was involved in a series of high-profile federal prosecutions, including ones against the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell and Sean "Diddy" Combs.Her lawsuit against the DOJ argued that her termination violated federal law and the Constitution and stemmed from President Donald Trump's longstanding animus toward her father, whom Trump had fired as FBI director in 2017.James Comey is currently under federal indictment that accuses him of threatening Trump's life by posting on Instagram a photo of seashells forming the number "86 47." His attorneys are seeking to have that case tossed out. James Comey, who denies any wrongdoing, previously had another federal indictment against him filed by the DOJ under Trump dismissed.Maurene Comey's suit said the DOJ did not give "any explanation whatsoever for terminating Ms. Comey," and, "In truth, there is no legitimate explanation.""Rather, Defendants fired Ms. Comey solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B. Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both," the suit said.Furman, in his ruling for Comey, referenced that claim, but his decision was based on other grounds.The judge rejected the DOJ's arguments that then-Attorney General Pam Bondi could remove a federal prosecutor "at will" and without cause and that current Attorney General Todd Blanche could ratify that act after the fact as he did in May as acting attorney general.Furman also rejected the DOJ's argument that even if the Civil Service Reform Act requires removal of a prosecutor for cause, an attorney general's firing of her constituted an implicit determination that she was removed "for such cause as will promote the efficiency of the service.""The Court need not dwell long on Defendants' second statutory argument justifying Comey's removal," Furman said, referring to that claim. "That is because the argument borders on frivolous."The judge noted that Comey was fired despite having had excellent performance reviews."Comey's supervisors and peers consistently lauded her work, describing her as a 'brilliant lawyer and a gifted supervisor,' 'the lawyer the office turns to when legal excellence is a must,' and 'an outstanding AUSA in every respect' with 'judgment, work product, and courtroom advocacy [that are] among the finest in the country,'" Furman wrote.The DOJ admitted that Comey's termination "was not 'for cause' and was not based on herperformance," Furman noted.In addition, the judge said, the DOJ's argument that Comey's termination was lawful ignored parts of the Civil Service Reform Act, which "required that Comey be given advance written notice (subject to certain exceptions not relevant here); 'a reasonable time' to respond orally and in writing; representation; and 'a written decision and the specific reasons therefor at the earliest practicable date.'""Defendants concede, as they must, that Comey was not afforded these procedural protections," the judge said.Furman also said the DOJ all but admitted that its argument that the attorney general had power to fire Comey under Article II of the U.S. Constitution — which establishes the executive branch of government — sought "to overturn nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent.""This Court, however, is bound to follow the Supreme Court's precedents unless and until the Supreme Court overturns them," Furman wrote.The DOJ, in a statement, said, "The Department disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course."That appeal would happen after Furman issues a final judgment in the case. The judge reserved judgment on Comey's claim that her firing violated her First Amendment rights. Furman gave her until Nov. 9 to file arguments on why that claim should not be dismissed as moot given his order in her favor on other grounds. CNBC has requested comment on the ruling from the White House. Comey, in a note to colleagues at the U.S. Attorney's Office after she was fired, wrote, "If a career prosecutor can be fired without reason, fear may seep into the decisions of those who remain.""Fear is the tool of a tyrant, wielded to suppress independent thought. Instead of fear, let this moment fuel the fire that already burns in the heart of this place," she wrote. "A fire of righteous indignation at abuses of power. Of commitment to seek justice for victims."

schema.headline: Trump DOJ unlawfully fired Epstein prosecutor Maurene Comey, judge rules

title: DOJ charges ex-FBI Director James Comey in new case
description: FILE PHOTO: Former FBI Director James Comey testified in front of the Senate Intelligence Committee in the Senate Hart building on Capitol Hill, on Th
body: FILE PHOTO: Former FBI Director James Comey testified in front of the Senate Intelligence Committee in the Senate Hart building on Capitol Hill, on Thursday, June 8, 2017.Cheriss May | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesFormer FBI Director James Comey has been charged for the third time with federal crimes, according to a court filing unsealed Monday in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., at Comey's request.Comey is accused in the new case with knowingly communicating information related to national defense to a person not entitled to receive it.He is also charged with conspiring with others to violate the law against sharing such information. The charging document, known as an information, says Comey, "through one or more co-conspirators," directed an unnamed individual "to disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication."According to a court filing by Comey, who is seeking to dismiss the new case, the information relates to the "alleged disclosure of classified information" to The New York Times on Oct. 5, 2016.Comey's lawyers told a judge in that filing that the alleged disclosure "was investigated by two separate U.S. Attorneys over the past ten years. Both declined to prosecute."Comey has been repeatedly targeted by the Department of Justice under the administration of President Donald Trump, who fired him as FBI director in 2017. Both men have been fierce critics of one another since then.The DOJ filed the information against Comey on Oct. 5 and asked a judge to seal it, citing the risk that an ongoing criminal investigation would be compromised by the charges becoming public. Judge Trevor McFadden granted that request that day.Attorneys for Comey, whom the DOJ agreed should be notified of the information, filed a motion to dismiss the case on Oct. 9, arguing that the 10-year statute of limitations to file a grand jury indictment relating to events of Oct. 5, 2016, had expired.Comey's lawyers accused the DOJ of filing "a faulty information under seal" in an effort to put the statute of limitations on hold.The attorneys on Monday asked McFadden to unseal the information, and the judge agreed to do so.Comey separately is currently seeking the dismissal of an indictment obtained by the DOJ in North Carolina federal court on charges of threatening Trump's life by posting a photo of seashells on a beach on social media. He previously successfully won dismissal of another indictment accusing him of falsely testifying to Congress.The new criminal complaint came to light hours after a federal judge in New York ruled that the Department of Justice had unlawfully fired Comey's daughter, Maurene Comey, last year as an assistant U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York."Well, they're back — again," James Comey said in a video message on Substack addressing the new case."It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to," he said. "Nothing's changed with me. I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary.""And I'm still lucky to have an amazing family and an incredible group of lawyers that will stand up in court and fight the latest and whatever comes after this," Comey said. "The next couple of years are going to be hard for all of us. It's really important that we stand straight and keep the faith in America."In the pending indictment in North Carolina, Comey in late April was charged with threatening Trump's life by posting on Instagram a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to form the numbers "86 47."Prosecutors claim that the number "86" — which is often used in restaurants to indicate a menu item is no longer available — was code for suggesting someone kill Trump, who is the 47th U.S. president.Comey has denied any wrongdoing in that case and is seeking to have the indictment tossed out by a judge.Comey was first indicted in September 2025 by a federal grand jury in Virginia on charges of making a false statement and obstruction, in connection with testimony he gave before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Sept. 30, 2020. Comey, in that testimony, denied authorizing another person at the FBI to serve as an anonymous source in news reports regarding an investigation of Hillary Clinton and her emails when she was the Democratic presidential nominee in 2016.That first indictment was dismissed by a judge on Nov. 24, 2025, after the judge ruled that Lindsey Halligan, a then-interim U.S. attorney who obtained the indictments, had been invalidly appointed. On the same day the judge tossed Comey's case for that reason, the same judge dismissed an unrelated indictment obtained by Halligan against New York Attorney General Letitia James, who had been accused of bank fraud and making false statements to a financial institution in connection with a home mortgage she obtained in 2020.James, like Comey, has been a staunch critic of Trump, and a target of the president's ire.

schema.headline: DOJ charges ex-FBI Director James Comey in new case

title: China industrial profits post strongest growth in three months, rising 14.4%
description: QIANDONGNAN, CHINA - OCTOBER 24: Workers produce jewelry products to fulfill orders at a workshop ahead of the upcoming Double 11 shopping festival on
body: QIANDONGNAN, CHINA - OCTOBER 24: Workers produce jewelry products to fulfill orders at a workshop ahead of the upcoming Double 11 shopping festival on October 24, 2026 in Congjiang County, Qiandongnan Miao and Dong Autonomous Prefecture, Guizhou Province of China.Shi Honghui | Visual China Group | Getty ImagesChina's industrial profits grew at their strongest pace last month since June, as a boom in manufacturing tied to artificial intelligence offset drag from persistently weak domestic demand.Profits at large industrial firms rose 14.4% in September from a year earlier, according to data released Tuesday by the National Bureau of Statistics. For the first nine months of this year, industrial profits climbed 15.5%, slightly below the 15.7% rise in the January-September period. The strength comes as industrial earnings swung to double-digit growth earlier this year, following a modest gain in 2025 after three straight years of declines, helped by Beijing's efforts to curb rampant price wars across sectors and surging demand for AI-related equipment.  The global AI boom and higher commodity prices stemming from the war in Iran have lifted earnings at miners, chipmakers and raw-material suppliers this year, even as downstream manufacturers face rising input costs and weak domestic demand.Earnings growth in high-tech sectors, such as AI and robotics, has been outperforming profits in consumer-related industries, including clothing, autos and furniture. NBS Chief Statistician Yu Weining attributed the growth mostly to surging profits in electronics and advanced-technology manufacturing sectors. Electronic special materials' manufacturers saw profits more than triple, while they jumped 51.7% for semiconductor device equipment makers, as demand for AI computing power and storage over the nine months remained robust. The buildout of AI computing power and data centers sent profits at optical fiber manufacturers more than sixfold higher, while those at cable makers more than doubled in the January to September period from a year earlier, according to Yu. Raw material producers for copper and aluminum also benefited from rising demand from AI-related and renewable industries, with profits expanding nearly 45% over the nine months.   watch nowHigh-tech manufacturing investment and electronics capacity utilization remain resilient, supported by the global AI cycle and domestic policy priorities, said Shena Yue, senior economist at Oxford Economics. Overall investment and industrial utilization are still subdued, she said.Household demand is the weak link as the property downturn continues to weigh on housing purchases and related durables, Yue said. "China's export strength isn't able to fully offset its domestic weakness," she said.China's economy expanded 4.5% in the third quarter from a year earlier, slightly faster than the previous quarter, taking growth in the first nine months to 4.6%, within the government's full-year target range of 4.5% to 5%. Consumption remains soft, with retail sales growing 1.1% in September, beating forecasts but only marginally above August's weak reading. With concerns mounting over local government debt and the benefits of consumer trade-in subsidies fading, Beijing has so far held back from major new stimulus for domestic demand.

schema.headline: China industrial profits post strongest growth in three months, rising 14.4%

title: Bessent dines at Cheesecake Factory, slams Obama over Trump joke
description: Scott Bessent, U.S. Treasury secretary, during an announcement on Trump Accounts in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Wedne
body: Scott Bessent, U.S. Treasury secretary, during an announcement on Trump Accounts in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026.Annabelle Gordon | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesLet them eat cheesecake?Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday became the latest right-wing critic to accuse former President Barack Obama of elitism for mockingly comparing President Donald Trump's ostentatious White House renovations to the Cheesecake Factory.  But Bessent, a former hedge fund manager whose net worth has been estimated at around $600 million, put his money where his mouth is — dining at the chain restaurant and praising its food before giving the Democratic ex-president a slice of his mind."This is the man who built the museum [that] looks like Darth Vader's tomb," Bessent told a Fox Business reporter who asked about Obama's remark as he left the restaurant near the White House. Bessent was apparently referring to the Obama Presidential Center, a monolithic structure that opened in June."I had a great meal, always have a great meal, and I would just tell the Martha's Vineyard set to give it a try," Bessent said. Obama vacationed on Martha's Vineyard as president, and he and his wife Michelle now own an estate on the exclusive island.Bessent said he ordered "what I always have: the French Dip Cheeseburger."That's a "Charbroiled Cheeseburger Served on a Toasted Brioche Roll with Grilled Onions, Sriracha Mayo and Au Jus for Dipping," one of the "Glamburgers" on Cheesecake Factory's famously sprawling menu. The burger, which comes with French fries or a green salad, currently costs $22.95 at the restaurant's downtown Washington location.The Cheesecake Factory is seen on May 02, 2025 in Arlington, Virginia. Kayla Bartkowski | Getty Images"I recommend the Cheeseburger Spring Rolls," Bessent added in a follow-up post on X directed at Obama.Bessent's biting comment followed those of other Trump allies who claim Obama sneered at working-class Americans when he tore into Trump over his extensive White House construction and decoration projects."I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV!" Obama said of Trump during a speech at an Ohio rally for gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton and Senate candidate Sherrod Brown on Saturday."There's gold everywhere. What's up with the gold?" Obama went on. "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."Former US President Barack Obama speaks during a midterm campaign rally as he campaigns alongside Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit, Michigan on Oct. 24, 2026. Bill Pugliano | AFP | Getty ImagesThe crowd erupted in cheers and laughter at the remarks from Obama, who has previously poked fun at Trump's gold-heavy remodel of the White House. Since retaking office, Trump has devoted significant amounts of time to discussing his renovations, including in the Oval Office, which now features heaps of gold leaf among many additional decorations. He has also built a White House helipad, the still-under-construction White House ballroom and an array of other projects.Trump on Monday afternoon defended his White House redesign at length while claiming Obama had failed to address needed repairs."We have to explain to Obama that the White House is a symbol of America, and it has to be maintained properly," Trump said as he headed to Mississippi for a campaign rally. "Guys like Obama don't see it. You don't see dirt. He doesn't see filth. He doesn't see broken ornaments on a building.""It has to be clean," Trump continued. "The columns can't be broken. The bricks can't be falling off from under the plaster. And for you to say it's a cheesecake factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president."Detractors insisted Obama's use of the Cheesecake Factory as an example of cheap, gaudy decor amounted to no less than class warfare."Classic Obama snobbery," Republican commentator Matt Whitlock wrote on X. "Cheesecake Factory is a great option for people who can't afford a private chef at their Martha's Vineyard estate."GOP pundit Scott Jennings called Obama "undefeated at condescending to regular folks," while claiming the former president "has never been in a Cheesecake Factory."That backlash quickly sparked its own backlash."This is actually a condescending view of working-class people," wrote Derek Guy, a popular menswear influencer, on X."I grew up in a working-class immigrant family and we ate at Red Lobster and The Cheesecake Factory for 'fancy nights out.' But even we understood that the White House should not look like the inside of a Red Lobster," Guy wrote. "Working-class people are not culturally illiterate just because their experiences are shaped by their limited means."The food fight is taking place just days before the Nov. 3 midterm election, where most polls and analyst projections indicate Democrats are poised to make significant gains in Congress. The election cycle has been defined by Americans' widespread unhappiness with high costs, which has dragged Trump's approval ratings to new lows and imperiled Republicans' majorities in the House and Senate.The Cheesecake Factory is set to report its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday.

schema.headline: Bessent dines at Cheesecake Factory, slams Obama over Trump joke

title: Prediction market traders say an Anthropic IPO is near-certain this year after company filed with SEC
description: watch nowAnthropic on Monday unveiled its Form S-1 filing, taking the company one step closer to completing its long-awaited move to the public market
body: watch nowAnthropic on Monday unveiled its Form S-1 filing, taking the company one step closer to completing its long-awaited move to the public markets, which is now seen as almost guaranteed to come this year. Speculators on prediction market platform Kalshi place 95% odds that the artificial intelligence giant officially announces an initial public offering by the end of 2026.  Kalshi defines officially announcing an IPO as either the Securities and Exchange Commission declaring an S-1 effective, a priced IPO or an exchange assigning a ticker to a stock. The Anthropic S-1 envisions a Nasdaq Stock Market ticker symbol of "ANT." Anthropic is aiming to start trading the week of Nov. 16, according to a report in the Wall Street Journal. Traders on Kalshi place just a 14% chance that the company begins trading before then. On the Polymarket platform, traders give a 69% chance that Anthropic will list on a public exchange and open for trading by Nov. 20. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Prediction market traders say an Anthropic IPO is near-certain this year after company filed with SEC

title: Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital
description: watch nowInvesting giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager su
body: watch nowInvesting giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity. The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.  Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.  For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconApollo Global Management, YTDJohn Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever. "Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.

schema.headline: Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital

title: Apple responds to user reports of broken iPhone Duo screens on new foldable phone
description: The Apple iPhone Duo smartphone at Apple's Fifth Avenue store during the first day of in-store sales in New York, US, on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. Michae
body: The Apple iPhone Duo smartphone at Apple's Fifth Avenue store during the first day of in-store sales in New York, US, on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesApple's first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, hit store shelves on Friday to considerable lines and long wait times for pre-orders. But some customers who were lucky enough to get the $1,999-and-up phone on its first weekend have been reporting a pretty big problem: The inner screen of the phone can break, showing horizontal bright lines emanating from the phone's hinge.Apple on Monday said it was aware of the issue, which it said affected a "small number" of phones, and that it would replace the devices under its AppleCare warranty. "We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units," an Apple representative told CNBC. "If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement."Apple says on its website that an inner-screen repair will be $999 for iPhone Duos that are out-of-warranty. Most of the reports are from anonymous customers on online forums such as Reddit and X, and there are fake images online as well. But well-respected device repair firm iFixit weighed in on Sunday, after tearing down the new device and testing its resistance to dust, and theorized the issues may have to do with Apple's hinge design."Many of these damage reports describe folding or unfolding the phone, hearing a crunch, and pushing past it," said iFixit technician Shahram Mokhtari in its teardown video. "Right where the damage is happening, the hinge is shaped a little differently.""The hinge is actually dozens of parts, with ludicrous precision," iFixit CEO Kyle Wiens posted on X. "A manufacturing variance or grain of sand can kill the fragile display panel it protects."watch nowBreaking screens have been an issue with foldable phones going back to 2019, and have been seen as one of the major roadblocks to the technology's widespread adoption. That year, Samsung released one of its first folding devices, and reviewers quickly found that its inner screen cracked during normal use. Early reviewers praised the experience of using the iPhone Duo when unfolded, especially for multitasking or media, but said that many apps had not been updated to take full advantage of the phone's larger and wider screens.Apple said on Monday that apps were already being updated for the new foldable device. "The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor," an Apple representative said in a statement.

schema.headline: Apple responds to user reports of broken iPhone Duo screens on new foldable phone

title: Trump says he'll soon decide whether to ‘make a deal’ with Iran or ‘finish it off'
description: US President Donald Trump speaks to reporters before boarding Marine One as he departs the White House for Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, en route to F
body: US President Donald Trump speaks to reporters before boarding Marine One as he departs the White House for Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, en route to Fort Myers, Florida, on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, DC, US, October 23, 2026.Evan Vucci | ReutersU.S. President Donald Trump has said he was deciding whether to "make a deal" with Iran or "finish it off" as investors weigh heightened tensions across the Middle East."Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal? It's getting to be decision time," Trump said in a Fox News interview on Sunday.Mediators from Qatar, which has played a key role in efforts to negotiate an agreement between Washington and Tehran, visited Tehran on Sunday, according to Reuters. It comes as attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants on Saudi Arabia continued over the weekend.The last confirmed U.S. strikes on Iran were on Sept. 1. Trump previously said attacks would not resume until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Tehran says it is preparing a military response to any U.S. strikes.A potential U.S. target could be Pickaxe Mountain, a deeply buried site linked to Iran's nuclear program, Trump said in the Sunday interview."We can read the badge on somebody's shirt from space, okay? We know exactly what's going on at Pickaxe Mountain. We know the other three [nuclear sites] are obliterated," Trump said.Trump also repeated the claim that the U.S. controls the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for global trade and a major flashpoint in the conflict, citing that crude oil flows have returned to prewar levels.Energy prices nonetheless remain elevated amid the disruption and a global refining squeeze.Washington and Tehran have both repeatedly claimed they control the route, where overall trade flows remain severely curtailed, impacting consumer prices.A Singapore-flagged container ship sank in the strait earlier this month after being struck by an unidentified projectile and catching fire.Ali Ozmaei, chief of the Iran Revolutionary Guard navy, said earlier this month that Tehran is "counting the moments" until it can sink American warships.Regional powers seek Iran talksSenior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are meeting Iran's leadership in Tehran on MondayThe three countries signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in August, committing to closer defense cooperation and stipulating that an armed attack against one member would be regarded as an attack against all.It is the first meeting of the group since Houthi missiles and drones targeted sites across Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh airport and an administrative building belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco.Saudi Arabia last week postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference until 2027 due to security concerns after a string of fatal strikes.

schema.headline: Trump says he'll soon decide whether to ‘make a deal’ with Iran or ‘finish it off'
